title: Linux for engineers
summary: Navigate, secure, package, schedule and troubleshoot a Linux server the way production work demands.
why: Every server, container and cloud VM you will debug runs it, so this is where most incidents are solved.

title: Git and version control
summary: Track changes with Git: commits, branches, merging, rebase, remotes, pull requests, tags, hooks, large repositories, and recovery when things go wrong.
why: It is how every change is reviewed, traced and rolled back, so you can say exactly what changed and when.

title: Shell scripting
summary: Write Bash scripts that fail loudly, run safely, parse JSON from APIs and replace repetitive manual work.
why: It turns a 20-minute manual fix into a script you can trust, test and hand to the next on-call.

title: Python for automation
summary: Write Python scripts that handle files, processes, HTTP APIs and cloud SDKs, with tests and a packaged command-line tool.
why: It is the glue for automation, tooling and data work, and the language most ops scripts outgrow bash into.

title: Networking essentials
summary: Reason about addresses, DNS, HTTP, TLS and firewalls well enough to debug any connectivity failure.
why: Most outages that look like app bugs are DNS, routing or firewall faults, and this is how you tell.

title: Docker and containers
summary: Build small, secure images, run multi-container applications, and understand registries, runtimes and the OCI standard.
why: Containers are how software ships today, so you need to build, run and debug them without guessing.

title: CI/CD and delivery
summary: Design pipelines that build, test and ship safely, secure the supply chain, and deploy with rolling, canary and declarative delivery.
why: A reliable pipeline is the difference between releasing on a Friday with confidence and not releasing at all.

title: Kubernetes
summary: Run workloads on Kubernetes from architecture and networking to Helm, autoscaling, operators, cluster upgrades, RBAC, troubleshooting and exam strategy.
why: It runs most production workloads, and the day it misbehaves you need a mental model, not a cheat sheet.

title: Terraform and infrastructure as code
summary: Describe infrastructure as code, use advanced HCL, manage state and secrets safely, and build real AWS and Azure stacks.
why: Infrastructure you cannot recreate from code is infrastructure you cannot safely change.

title: Cloud platforms: AWS and Azure
summary: Core concepts side by side on AWS and Azure: identity, networks, DNS and CDN, compute, serverless, managed Kubernetes, security, monitoring and cost.
why: Cloud accounts hold the money, the data and the blast radius, so knowing the core services pays off daily.

title: Observability
summary: Instrument systems with metrics, logs and traces, ship them with OpenTelemetry, probe from outside, and alert on what users actually feel.
why: You cannot fix what you cannot see, and this is what makes a 3am page a ten-minute fix.

title: Site reliability engineering
summary: Define reliability with SLOs, respond to incidents, run on-call, plan capacity, practise failure and manage change safely.
why: It gives reliability a number, a budget and a method, so arguments about risk become decisions.

title: DevSecOps and security
summary: Build security into delivery: threat modeling, secrets, pipeline and supply chain checks, container and Kubernetes hardening, cloud identity and incident response.
why: A breach costs far more than the checks that prevent it, and these habits fit inside normal delivery.

title: Ansible and configuration management
summary: Describe servers in inventories and playbooks, keep them consistent with idempotent roles, protect secrets with Vault and roll changes out safely.
why: It keeps fleets of machines configured the same way without logging in to each one.

title: Databases for operators
summary: Run relational databases with confidence: SQL, indexes and plans, transactions, backups, replication, safe migrations, caches and incident triage.
why: The database is usually the slowest and least forgiving part of an outage, so operators need its basics.

title: Go for DevOps engineers
summary: Write small, fast, reliable Go services and tools: types, errors, interfaces, goroutines, context, HTTP, testing, containers and debugging.
why: Much of the cloud tooling you use is written in Go, so reading and writing it makes you self-sufficient.

title: Helm for beginners
summary: Package, configure, upgrade and roll back Kubernetes applications with Helm: charts, values, templates, releases, dependencies and debugging.
why: It is the standard way to package and version Kubernetes apps, and you will meet it in most clusters.

title: Cloud security and IAM
summary: Control who and what can do what in the cloud: identities, roles and policies on AWS and Azure, least privilege, secrets and keys, private networking, audit logs and debugging access errors.
why: Most cloud breaches are permission mistakes, so least privilege is the cheapest control you have.

title: Kubernetes administration and operations
summary: Run clusters, not only apps: control plane and etcd, backups, safe upgrades, RBAC, node maintenance, quotas and autoscaling, network and pod security, and debugging cluster faults.
why: Running the cluster itself, with upgrades, backups and RBAC, is the work that separates users from operators.

title: Continuous delivery with Argo CD
summary: Deliver to Kubernetes by letting a controller pull the desired state from a repository: applications, sync and drift, Helm and Kustomize, environments, hooks, access and debugging.
why: Git as the source of truth for what runs lets you roll back by reverting a commit.

title: LLM fundamentals
summary: Understand how large language models work in practice: tokens, context windows, sampling, training, API calls, cost, latency, evaluation and debugging.
why: You cannot judge or secure an AI feature without knowing how these models work and where they fail.

title: Prompting and structured output
summary: Write reliable prompts, give examples, ask for step-by-step reasoning, get validated JSON back, and version and test your prompts.
why: Reliable prompts and structured output turn a clever demo into a component you can depend on.

title: Claude Skills
summary: Package expertise as skills Claude loads on demand: SKILL.md, descriptions that trigger, progressive disclosure, scripts, testing, sharing and security.
why: Reusable skills capture your team's know-how once so every run follows it the same way.

title: Tool use and MCP
summary: Let models call tools safely: function calling, the tool-use loop, the Model Context Protocol, building a server, permissions and prompt injection.
why: It is the common plug for giving AI tools safe, narrow access to your systems and data.

title: System design for platform and SRE
summary: Design systems that fail small: estimation, caching, queues, consistency, quorums, cells, shuffle sharding, load shedding, multi-region, change safety, and worked designs reviewed against real outages.
why: Design reviews and interviews both reward the same skill: reasoning about load, failure and trade-offs.

title: MLOps: machine learning in production
summary: Run models like any other production system: data checks, reproducible training, tested pipelines, a model registry, safe releases, serving, and monitoring for drift with a retraining loop.
why: Models decay silently in production, so you need versioning, monitoring and safe release habits.

title: AIOps: algorithms for operations
summary: Use statistics and machine learning to help run systems: anomaly detection, alert correlation, log and trace patterns, root cause hints, incident assistants and safe auto-remediation.
why: Alert noise is the main cause of on-call burnout, and these methods cut it without hiding real incidents.

title: AIOps in practice
summary: Run AIOps safely: data pipelines, remediation tiers and verification, kill switches and audit, chaos tests, retrieval over runbooks, agents and approval gates, prompt injection, evaluation, build versus buy, failure modes and operations.
why: Automation that fixes things can also break things, so approval tiers, audit and kill switches come first.

title: Virtualization
summary: Understand hypervisors, CPU and memory overcommit, virtual disks and snapshots, virtual networks and live migration, and troubleshoot a KVM host.
why: Hypervisors still sit under most clouds and data centres, and their limits explain many odd outages.

title: Storage and filesystems
summary: Choose block, file or object storage, manage ext4 and XFS, LVM and RAID, NFS, iSCSI and Ceph, and diagnose slow or full disks.
why: Data loss is the failure you cannot undo, so understanding disks, filesystems and RAID matters early.

title: KubeVirt: VMs on Kubernetes
summary: Run virtual machines on Kubernetes: architecture, install, disks and CDI, storage and live migration, networking, performance, backup, operations and moving from VMware.
why: It lets you run legacy VMs beside containers, which is how many migrations actually happen.

title: Ceph and software-defined storage
summary: Understand and operate Ceph: RADOS, OSDs and monitors, CRUSH and placement groups, RBD, CephFS, RGW, Rook on Kubernetes, performance, failure recovery and capacity planning.
why: It is the open-source storage behind many private clouds, and it rewards teams who understand its failure modes.

title: Vault and secrets management
summary: Manage secrets with HashiCorp Vault: seal and unseal, auth methods, policies, KV, dynamic secrets, PKI, transit encryption, Kubernetes integration, high availability and incident response.
why: Secrets in config files and chat logs are a standing risk, and this is the clean way to replace them.

title: SQL performance and database operations
summary: Read query plans, add the right indexes, untangle locks, size connection pools and run replication, vacuum and day-two operations.
why: A slow query can take a whole service down, and reading a query plan is how you find out why.

title: GPU, AI infrastructure and LLM serving
summary: Know what limits inference on a GPU, run vLLM, TGI and Triton, schedule GPUs on Kubernetes, and control latency and cost.
why: GPUs are the costliest resource in the stack, so serving models efficiently is a financial skill too.

title: OpenStack and private cloud
summary: Run a private cloud: Keystone, Nova, Neutron, Cinder and Glance, quotas, scheduling, networking and day-two operations.
why: It is how large organisations run their own cloud, and the skills carry over to any IaaS.

title: Bare metal and datacenter
summary: Rack, provision and operate physical servers: BMC and IPMI, PXE provisioning, disks and RAID, leaf-spine networking and fleet operations.
why: When there is no cloud API, you still have to provision, patch and recover real hardware.

title: Service mesh and Kubernetes networking
summary: Understand pod networking, CNI and network policy, then run a service mesh with mTLS, traffic routing and troubleshooting.
why: It moves retries, encryption and traffic control out of every app and into the platform.

title: Reverse proxies and load balancers
summary: Run nginx, HAProxy and Envoy in front of services: routing, TLS, load balancing, timeouts, caching, rate limits and debugging 502 and 504 errors.
why: Load balancers and proxies sit in front of everything, so their settings decide what users actually see.

title: Messaging and streaming
summary: Choose and operate queues and logs: RabbitMQ and Kafka, delivery guarantees, consumer groups, lag, retention, schemas and managed cloud services.
why: Queues and streams decouple systems, and also hide the failures that pile up quietly behind them.

title: CloudFormation and Bicep
summary: Write and operate cloud-native infrastructure as code: AWS CloudFormation and Azure Bicep, change previews, stacks, modules, testing and debugging failed deployments.
why: Many employers run native infrastructure code, so reading CloudFormation or Bicep is a hiring skill.

title: Google Cloud
summary: Learn the Google Cloud model: projects, VPC, Compute Engine, Cloud Storage, GKE, Cloud Run, data and messaging services, operations and cost, with the gcloud CLI.
why: Google Cloud is the third major platform, and its networking and IAM model differs enough to need study.

title: Platform engineering
summary: Build the internal developer platform: golden paths, a developer portal and catalog, self-service workflows, platform APIs, guardrails, multi-tenancy, cost allocation, and the measures that show it helps.
why: Teams that share one well-built platform ship faster and safer than teams that each assemble their own.

title: CKA and CKS exam practice
summary: Task-based practice for the hands-on Kubernetes certifications: speed setup, imperative kubectl, cluster tasks, troubleshooting and the security domains, ending with a timed mock run.
why: The CKA and CKS are scored on what you can do at a terminal, and real clusters reward the same speed and accuracy.

title: Control plane and etcd internals
summary: How a request travels through the API server, how etcd stores and protects state, and how the scheduler, controllers and kubelet turn it into running pods.
why: When the control plane misbehaves everything slows or stops, and knowing each part tells you where to look first.

title: Cluster lifecycle and HA
summary: Design a highly available control plane, bootstrap with kubeadm, manage certificates, upgrade safely, replace nodes, back up etcd and rehearse recovery.
why: Clusters live for years, so upgrades, certificate expiry and recovery decide whether they stay healthy.

title: Kubernetes networking deep dive
summary: The network model, CNI plugins, Services and kube-proxy, EndpointSlices, CoreDNS, network policies, Ingress and the Gateway API, and a fixed method for debugging.
why: Most cluster outages show up as network symptoms, and a fixed debugging order finds the real cause quickly.

title: Resource management and autoscaling
summary: Requests, limits and QoS, CPU throttling and OOM, quotas and priority, eviction, HPA, VPA, node autoscaling with Karpenter and KEDA, and disruption planning.
why: Resource settings decide both your cloud bill and whether pods survive pressure, so they need measuring, not guessing.

title: Kubernetes security deep dive
summary: Threat modelling, identities and tokens, RBAC design, Pod Security and admission policy, secrets encryption, multi-tenancy, CIS hardening and incident response.
why: Clusters hold credentials and run untrusted code, so layered controls and a rehearsed response limit the damage of one mistake.

title: Observability in depth
summary: PromQL rates and recording rules, scaling Prometheus, SLO burn rate alerts, logs at scale with Loki, tracing and sampling, and observability as code with cost control.
why: Basic dashboards stop helping at scale, so you need correct queries, burn rate alerts and controlled cost.

title: Kubernetes supply chain and runtime security
summary: Supply chain threats and SLSA, image scanning, SBOMs and cosign signing, admission enforcement of provenance, Falco runtime detection, seccomp, AppArmor and sandboxed runtimes.
why: Most cluster compromises arrive inside an image, so verify what runs and detect what it does at runtime.

title: IaC beyond Terraform
summary: OpenTofu and ecosystem choices, Pulumi in real languages, Terragrunt structure, testing infrastructure code, policy as code and drift detection, and safe state migrations.
why: Teams outgrow one tool or one layout, so learn the alternatives, testing and policy that keep infrastructure code safe.

title: Behavioral and leadership track
summary: STAR stories, communicating technical decisions, influence without authority, mentoring and feedback, leading incidents, and growing into senior and staff scope.
why: Senior roles are decided on judgement and communication, which interviews test with stories you must prepare.

title: AI infrastructure in production
summary: GPU scheduling and sharing on Kubernetes, vector databases, RAG pipelines, LLM gateways, LLM observability and evaluation, and cost and capacity for inference.
why: AI features add GPUs, vector stores and token costs to your platform, and they need the same operations discipline.

title: Rust for infrastructure engineers
summary: Ownership and borrowing, errors with Result, structs enums and traits, CLI tools with clap and serde, async with tokio, and testing and shipping static binaries.
why: Rust gives fast, safe single binaries for agents and tools, and its model is worth understanding before you read the code.

title: Database operations in production
summary: PostgreSQL replication and failover, backups and point in time recovery, connection pooling, zero downtime migrations, Redis and MongoDB operations, and database incident runbooks.
why: Databases hold the data you cannot lose, so replication, restores and migrations must be practised before an incident.

title: Python for operations engineering
summary: Packaging and virtual environments, CLI tools, API clients with retries, concurrency, testing with pytest and safe cloud and Kubernetes SDK patterns.
why: Operations scripts become real tools, so they need packaging, tests, safe defaults and careful API handling.
